newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Child labor on the rise in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Child labor on the rise in Latin America.

text.p: Driven by poverty and economic upheaval, child labour is on the rise in Latin America where at least 15 million children under the age of 15 are working, officials said on Friday.

"Poverty is both cause and effect. Children are forced to work because they are poor and remain poor because they are forced to work," said Joao Carlos Alexim, director of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in Brazil.

An ILO report issued at a meeting of regional experts said the number of teenagers put to work in Latin America could be as high as 20 million, or one in every five children. It said 7.6 million children between 10-14 years had to work.
On average, they work 46 hours a week. Those that manage to go to school still face a 35-hour work week, it said.
Across Latin America, their health was being endangered in fields, mines, brick factories or chalk quarries.
"The life expectancy of the miners is relatively short; lung disease combined with tuberculosis harms and prematurely ends their lives," the ILO report said.
Children are also used as domestic servants or forced into prostitution, though data on this is scarse, the report said.
Representatives of non-governmental organisations, human rights groups and governments met to prepare for a world conference on child labour to be held in Norway in October.
Alexim told Reuters the growth in child labour in Latin America in the past decade was mainly due to poverty.
But structural changes in Latin American countries, as they open their economies to trade and give market forces free rein had also contributed to the increase.
Ecuador was the worst offender in the region with 30 percent of its children at work, according to 1994 figures.
In Guatemala the figure was 23.8 percent and in Brazil 20.5 percent, the report said.
But the ILO said most countries have taken steps to take children out of factories and fields and back into schools.
It praised Brazil for a programme that pays parents to send their children to class, and Colombia for having the clearest policies on child labour in the region.
Alexim said the child labour problem was worse elsewhere.
"Compared with Asia and Africa, I would say Latin America does not fare too badly. Nevertheless, the levels of child labour here are horrendous," he said.
